title: A signpost at every crossroads
allegory: A policy is like a signpost at every crossroads: a plain sign points one way (deterministic), a spinner sign shows the odds for each road (stochastic), and following the signs from any start gives a route.
map: the roads leading out of it
a plain signpost pointing one way
a spinner showing the odds for each road
a stochastic policy: π(a | s), a distribution over actions
repainting signs where a better road exists
policy improvement: act greedily on the value function

cap.1: An agent keeps landing in situations and must choose what to do next. The thing that makes that choice has a name: the policy.
cap.2: In an MDP the agent sees a state, takes an action, gets a reward and a new state. The policy is whatever maps the state it sees to the action it takes.
cap.3: A policy π is the agent's decision rule inside an MDP: a map from states to actions, π(s), or to distributions over actions, π(a | s).

cap.1: Picture a signpost at every crossroads. A plain sign points one way; a spinner sign gives odds, 70% left, 30% straight on. Follow the signs to get a route.
cap.2: A deterministic policy picks one action per state; a stochastic one gives a probability for each action. In ARENA's gridworld a deterministic policy is just an integer array.
cap.3: Deterministic: π: S → A, a length-|S| integer array in tabular code. Stochastic: π(a | s) with Σₐ π(a | s) = 1, which exploration and policy-gradient methods rely on.

cap.1: Read it as: the move is drawn from the policy's odds, given where you are. A plain signpost is the special case where one road gets all the odds.
cap.2: π(a | s) is the probability of taking action a in state s. A deterministic policy puts probability 1 on a single action, so it is a special case of the stochastic kind.
cap.3: A deterministic policy is the degenerate π(a | s) = 1[a = π(s)]. Stochastic policies can be parameterised, e.g. a softmax over logits, which makes them differentiable in θ.

chapters.name: A whole policy
chapters.title: A policy on a small gridworld: one action per square

cap.1: A whole policy on a tiny board: one arrow per square. Start bottom-left and the arrows walk you round the pit to the prize.
cap.2: A tabular policy is literally a lookup table, one action per state. ARENA's gridworld stores it as an integer array, which policy iteration keeps rewriting.
cap.3: Tabular deterministic π; policy iteration alternates exact evaluation, v = (I − γPπ)⁻¹rπ, with greedy improvement until the policy array stops changing.

chapters.name: Two ways to learn

right.title: learn the policy itself
lines: raise the odds of moves that worked

chapters.verdict: Either way, the policy is what finally acts.

cap.1: You can get good signposts two ways: score every road and point each sign at the best one, or nudge each spinner's odds towards moves that worked.
cap.2: Value-based methods (Q-learning, DQN) learn action values and act greedily. Policy-gradient methods (VPG, PPO) learn π directly. Both end with a policy that acts.
cap.3: Value-based: π(s) = argmax_a Q(s, a), implicit and deterministic. Policy-based: parameterise π_θ(a | s) and ascend expected return. Actor-critic methods learn both.

cap.1: A language model is a policy too. The text so far is where it stands, the next word is its move, and its word probabilities are the spinner.
cap.2: Treat each context as a state and each next token as an action: the LM's softmax output is a stochastic policy π(token | context). RLHF fine-tunes exactly this policy.
cap.3: An autoregressive LM is a stochastic policy over a token-level MDP; RLHF optimises π_θ against a reward model. Sampling temperature reshapes π at decode time.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Every agent acts through a policy
Signpost or spinner: deterministic or stochastic
Steering a model means changing its policy

cap.1: When you shape how an AI behaves, you are changing its policy: which move it makes in each situation. All of RL is about finding a better one.
cap.2: Q-learning, policy gradients, PPO and RLHF are all ways to improve π. Keep the roles straight: values score situations, policies act in them.
cap.3: RL optimises π for expected return. Alignment work, from RLHF to activation steering, is about which policy a model ends up with and whether it generalises as intended.

coda.title: Paint your own signposts: tap a square to turn its sign clockwise

readouts.label: walker from bottom-left
readouts.f: (() => { const D = [[-1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [0, -1]]; let r = 2, c = 0; const seen = new Set(); for (let t = 0; t < 20; t++) { if (r === 0 && c === 3) return 'reached the prize in ' + t + ' steps'; if (r === 1 && c === 3) return 'fell in the pit after ' + t + ' steps'; const key = r + ',' + c; if (seen.has(key)) return 'stuck going round in circles'; seen.add(key); const d = D[((G[r][c] % 4) + 4) % 4]; let nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1]; if (nr < 0 || nr > 2 || nc < 0 || nc > 3 || (nr === 1 && nc === 1)) { nr = r; nc = c; } r = nr; c = nc; } return 'wandered for 20 steps'; })()

readouts.label: return (+1 prize, −1 pit, −0.04 per step)
readouts.f: (() => { const D = [[-1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [0, -1]]; let r = 2, c = 0; const seen = new Set(); for (let t = 0; t < 20; t++) { if (r === 0 && c === 3) return (1 - 0.04 * t).toFixed(2); if (r === 1 && c === 3) return (-1 - 0.04 * t).toFixed(2); const key = r + ',' + c; if (seen.has(key)) return 'keeps paying 0.04 forever'; seen.add(key); const d = D[((G[r][c] % 4) + 4) % 4]; let nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1]; if (nr < 0 || nr > 2 || nc < 0 || nc > 3 || (nr === 1 && nc === 1)) { nr = r; nc = c; } r = nr; c = nc; } return (-0.8).toFixed(2); })()

caption.1: Each square's number is its sign: 0 up, 1 right, 2 down, 3 left. Tap to turn it and see where the walker ends up. Try steering it into the pit, or a loop.
caption.2: You are editing a deterministic tabular policy. The walker rolls it out from the start state; a policy that bumps a wall or cycles never reaches the prize.
caption.3: π: S → A as an integer table, rolled out with deterministic moves. Changing one state's action can change the whole trajectory and its return.

where_else: Language models: context is the state, the next token is the action, the softmax is the policy
Game-playing agents such as AlphaZero, whose network outputs a policy over moves
Thermostats and controllers: a fixed rule from reading to action
Policy iteration in [2.1], which rewrites a tabular policy until it stops changing

hamming.what: The agent's decision rule: a map from each state to an action, or to a probability for each action.
hamming.when: In every RL problem; it is what all RL algorithms, from Q-learning to PPO and RLHF, are trying to improve.
hamming.why: Values score situations, but only the policy acts, so it is where behaviour actually lives.

object.title: The spinner rack
object.subtitle: One row per crossroads, one bar per road; a single knob turns spinners into plain signposts and back.

cap.1: Each row is one crossroads and each bar one road; height is the chance of taking it. This is a stochastic policy.
cap.2: π(a | s) as a table: rows are states, columns are actions, and each row sums to 1.
cap.3: A softmax policy: π(a | s) ∝ exp(pref(s, a) / T).

cap.1: Turn the randomness down and every row becomes one tall bar. The spinners have become plain signposts.
cap.2: As T approaches 0 the policy becomes deterministic: the argmax of the preferences.
cap.3: Low temperature collapses π to 1[a = argmax pref]: a greedy, deterministic policy.

cap.1: Turn it up and every road becomes nearly equally likely. Good for exploring, bad for getting anywhere.
cap.2: High T spreads probability over all actions: maximum exploration.
cap.3: Large T tends to the uniform policy; PPO's entropy bonus pushes in this direction during training.

cap.1: From the front: a close call like s3 keeps two roads alive, while a clear case like s1 barely wavers.
cap.2: States with near-tied preferences stay stochastic the longest.
cap.3: A state's policy entropy depends on its preference gaps; small gaps mean high entropy at any given T.

cap.1: From above, a signpost policy is just one arrow per square: the lookup table you edit in the playground.
cap.2: The deterministic limit is the integer-array policy of tabular RL.
cap.3: Tabular π: S → A is the T → 0 limit of this softmax policy.

predict.q: A deterministic policy is best described as...
predict.why: A score for each state is the value function. The policy chooses actions.

predict.q: A language model generating text is acting as...

options.t: A stochastic policy over next tokens

predict.why: Context is the state, the next token is the action, and the softmax is π(a | s). RLHF trains exactly this policy.

predict.q: How does Q-learning end up with a policy?

options.t: By acting greedily on its learned Q-values

predict.why: Value-based methods read π off Q with an argmax; policy-gradient methods adjust π directly.

object.where: Any rule from situation to action: game agents, controllers, and language models picking tokens.
